idiom_name: iterator adapter chain consumed by a terminal method (sum/fold/collect/for)
implementation_notes: Rust's iteration protocol is this pattern absorbed into the language: the standard library documents that iterators and iterator adapters are lazy and that nothing really happens until next is called, so map/filter/flat_map/take_while build one composed iterator value with no allocation and no intermediate collection, ending in a consuming method (sum, fold, collect, for). Adapters are generic and monomorphized, so a chain over a slice normally compiles to the same machine loop a programmer would write; collect() is the deliberate materialization boundary, and try_fold/scan carry fallible or stateful stage logic without side effects inside adapters.
code_sketch:
let total: u64 = people.iter()
    .filter(|p| p.age > 18)
    .map(|p| p.score)
    .take(100)
    .sum();                    // one pass, no Vec allocated
pitfalls: collect() between stages materializes the whole intermediate Vec - the classic way a fused chain silently becomes the staged one.
Iterator adapters are lazy to the point of doing nothing: a chain of adapters with no consumer triggers the unused_must_use warning and performs no work.

Boxing the chain (Box<dyn Iterator<Item = T>>) or hiding adapters behind non-inlined trait objects re-introduces per-element dispatch and defeats the inlining that makes the chain cheap; prefer returning impl Iterator.
